tip: ‘dod â’ (literally come with) means bring: ‘daeth e â blodau’ = he brought flowers.
before I arrived uses ‘cyn i fi’ plus a softened verb: ‘cyrraedd’ becomes ‘gyrraedd’, giving ‘cyn i fi gyrraedd’.
Add ‘-ach’ for more and ‘na’ for than: ‘sych’ (dry) becomes ‘sychach’, and ‘sychach na'r llynedd’ = drier than last year.
‘dylwn i’ means I should and softens the verb: ‘bwyta’ becomes ‘fwyta’, so ‘dylwn i fwyta’ = I should eat.
Welsh has no verb for have; possession uses a form of ‘gan’: ‘roedd llais hyfryd ganddi’ = she had a lovely voice (‘ganddi’ = with her).
‘eisiau’ (to want) normally takes no ‘yn’ linker: ‘wyt ti eisiau bisgïen?’ = do you want a biscuit, not ‘wyt ti'n eisiau’.
‘arferai’ means used to and softens the verb: ‘cerdded’ becomes ‘gerdded’, so ‘arferai hi gerdded’ = she used to walk.
‘ga i...?’ asks may I have...? and softens the noun: ‘paned’ becomes ‘baned’, as in ‘ga i baned o de?’
‘alli di...?’ means can you...? and softens the verb: ‘pasio’ becomes ‘basio’, as in ‘alli di basio'r halen?’
South Welsh shows possession with ‘gyda’: ‘beiro gyda ti’ = you have a pen, literally a pen with you.
‘rhaid i’ (someone) means must, and the verb softens: ‘cymryd’ becomes ‘gymryd’, so ‘rhaid iddi hi gymryd’ = she must take.
here ‘a’ means whether in an indirect question: ‘gofynnodd e... a oeddwn i’ = he asked whether I was.
Front the key word for emphasis: ‘Cymraeg dw i eisiau dysgu’ = it is Welsh I want to learn, stressing ‘Cymraeg’.
‘na’ before a consonant, ‘nag’ before a vowel: ‘cryfach nag ydw i’ = stronger than I am, like English a and an.
‘roedd’ plus ‘wedi’ marks a had-done past: ‘roeddwn i wedi anghofio’ = I had forgotten.
‘heb’ plus a verb means not done: ‘heb ei bostio’ = without having posted it.
‘pe bai’ sets up an unreal if: ‘pe bai'r plant yn dawel’ = if the children were quiet, implying they are not.
as...as is ‘mor’ plus adjective plus ‘â’, or ‘ag’ before a vowel: ‘mor brydferth ag eos’ = as beautiful as a nightingale.
Welsh has two you forms: ‘ti’ (informal) as in ‘gallet ti’, and ‘chi’ (formal or plural).
After ‘rhaid i’ (someone), the verb softens: ‘brysio’ becomes ‘frysio’ in ‘rhaid i ni frysio’.
‘rhaid’ itself stays the same across tenses; the ‘bod’ part changes: ‘rhaid i ni’ (must), ‘roedd rhaid i ni’ (had to).
‘ga i’ (may I, or can I have) softens what follows: ‘gweld’ becomes ‘weld’, as in ‘ga i weld’.
‘cyn i’ plus a subject and verb means before someone does: ‘cyn iddi dywyllu’ = before it gets dark.
‘dylai’ means should or ought to: ‘dylai fe ymweld’ = he should visit.
‘ar ôl i’ plus a subject and verb means after someone does: ‘ar ôl iddyn nhw fynd’ = after they left.
‘yma’ (this) and ‘yna’ (that) sit after the noun: ‘y llyfr yma’ = this book, ‘yr un yna’ = that one.
For comparatives use ‘yn fwy’ (more) plus ‘na’ for than: ‘yn fwy cyfforddus na'r hen un’ = more comfortable than the old one.
Unreal conditions pair ‘pe’ (if) with ‘byddwn i’ (I would): ‘pe gallwn i ddewis, byddwn i'n byw’.
The south says ‘gyda’ for have: ‘profiad gyda ti’ = you have experience; the north uses ‘gen’ or ‘gan’.
For longer adjectives, most is ‘mwyaf’ placed before the word: ‘y person mwyaf cyfeillgar’ = the friendliest person.
